tip: Use 'till' for what you eat at a meal: 'köttbullar till lunch' = meatballs for lunch.
'Jobba' is the casual word for work, as in 'han jobbar'. 'Arbeta' means the same but sounds more formal.
Swedish 'i' marks a span of time: 'väntar i fem minuter' = wait for five minutes.
After 'en' the adjective keeps its base form: 'en ny dator'; a neuter noun would force 'nytt'.
'Fika' is the Swedish coffee-and-cake break, both noun and verb: 'äter fika' = have a fika.
Professions drop the article ('han är kock'), but add 'en' once an adjective appears: 'en bra kock'.
To want a thing, add 'ha': 'vill ha vatten' = want water. 'Vill' alone only pairs with another verb.
Counting up: 'en, två, tre, fyra, fem'. Watch 'två' (tvoh) – the 'å' sounds like the o in 'more'.
A container of something often takes 'med': 'en tallrik med köttbullar' = a plate of meatballs.
'Sätta sig' means sit down and is reflexive: 'vi sätter oss' uses 'oss' to match 'vi' (we).
'Varannan' means every other: 'tvättar kläder varannan dag' = every other day.
Taking transport uses the definite form: 'tar bussen' = take the bus, literally take the-bus.
A glass of water needs no linking word: 'ett glas vatten', the two nouns just sit together.
'Var' before a time unit means 'every': 'var femtonde minut' = every fifteen minutes.
'Lättöl' is one word, from 'lätt' (light) plus 'öl' (beer); Swedish freely glues words together.
A neuter ('ett') noun forces '-t' on the adjective: 'ett stort kontor', not 'stor'.
'Titta' needs 'på' to watch something: 'tittar på TV' = watch TV.
'Tycker' states an opinion or taste; use 'tror' for belief or a guess: 'vi tycker att filmen var bra'.
'På lördag' means this coming Saturday; add '-ar' ('på lördagar') for every Saturday.
In a main clause, adverbs like 'alltid' usually sit right after the verb: 'dricker alltid kaffe'.
'Te' (tea) becomes 'teet' once the definite ending is added: 'socker i teet' = sugar in the tea.
'Lyssna' takes 'på' before what you hear: 'lyssnar på musik' = listen to music.
'Halv åtta' means 7:30, not 8:30. Swedish counts toward the next hour, so it is literally half to eight.
'Byta' means change or switch: 'byta tåg' = change trains, with no article on 'tåg'.
'Duktig' takes 'på att' before a verb: 'duktig på att laga mat' = good at cooking.
Swedish normally repeats the article for each noun: 'en bror och en syster', not one 'en' for both.
'Borde' (should) is a helper verb, so the next verb is a plain infinitive with no 'att': 'borde gå bra'.
'God' means good-tasting for food, while 'bra' is good in general: 'god mat' = tasty food.
Date ordinals usually end in '-de' or '-te': 'femtonde' = fifteenth, as in 'den femtonde mars'.
'Middag' looks like English 'midday' but means dinner, the evening meal, as in 'vi äter middag klockan sex'.
